New York City Ballet, or NYCB, is an American ballet company founded in nineteen forty-eight by choreographer George Balanchine and Lincoln Kirstein, establishing New York as a global center for ballet innovation. The company pioneered a distinctly American approach to classical ballet: faster-paced, stripped of narrative ornamentation, and grounded in pure movement. It remains one of the world's most influential ballet institutions, defining twentieth-century dance aesthetics.

The company was co-founded by George Balanchine, a Russian émigré choreographer who revolutionized ballet technique and aesthetics. It was established in New York during the Cold War era, asserting American cultural leadership in classical dance. The company created a signature style emphasizing musicality, speed, and geometric precision, departing from narrative-heavy Russian Imperial ballet.

Jerome Robbins co-founded the company and served as ballet master, creating major works that blended classical training with American vernacular movement. His contributions helped define the company's innovative approach. The company collaborated extensively with composer Igor Stravinsky, commissioning and premiering numerous ballets that defined the late-twentieth-century canon.

Balanchine developed the Balanchine body, a training methodology emphasizing long lines, turnout, and the illusion of weightlessness. Dancers trained in this method look distinctive—ethereal and precise. The company is known for rapid-fire choreography and rapid ballet speeds that pushed technical demands far beyond traditional European conventions. This demanding approach became the hallmark of New York City Ballet style.

The company remains a training ground for dancers who influence ballet companies globally, maintaining Balanchine's choreographic legacy long after his death. George Balanchine is the visionary founder whose aesthetic shaped the company's entire mission. Jerome Robbins was a co-founder and prolific choreographer who bridged classical ballet and American musical theater. Igor Stravinsky was the primary compositional collaborator, with multiple premieres of his works.

The company exemplifies modernist transformation of classical technique. The artistic movement of modernism is embodied in dance form through the company's innovations. The United States is the nation whose cultural identity became intertwined with the company's success and innovation. The Cold War was the historical context in which American ballet became a cultural asset and assertion of Western modernity. New York City Ballet represents all of these forces coming together.
